name: The Cook household — a documented baker, unplaced in the town
head: cook_j_b

arrival.note: A BOUND FROM THE PAPER, NOT AN ARRIVAL. The corpus first prints this person at the Democrat of 5 November 1834, column 9, so they are in the town's paper by 1834-11-05 and at no stated time before it; nothing reached says when they came. Last printed 1834-11-05.

lives_at.note: Not attested. NOTHING IS BEING WITHHELD HERE: no source reached says where this person lived, and 52 households in this dataset were already in that position before this one was written.

works_at.note: Not attested as a structure this project models. The trade is documented; the premises are not one of the committed records.

present_on_scene_date.note: THE CORPUS STOPS BEFORE THE SCENE DATE. Last printed 1834-11-05, at the Democrat of 5 November 1834, column 9, and nothing reached either follows this person to 1 July 1835 or says they left. A documented resident whose whereabouts on one day are unknown is `uncertain` here rather than dropped: that is the same distinction index.json draws for Jeremiah Porter, and it is a finding rather than a gap.

persons.name: J. B. Cook

occupation.note: THE TRADE IS THE PAPER'S. The corpus reads it as baker, at the Democrat of 5 November 1834, column 9. The residents vocabulary's nearest period-correct word for it is `baker`, and where the corpus prints more than one trade they are all named here rather than reduced to the one the vocabulary could take.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'JB. COOK' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 5 November 1834, column 9. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `baker` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

merge_ruling.for_merge: 'J. B. Cook', a documented baker from the Democrat of 5 November 1834, shares a surname with both.
merge_ruling.against_merge: The initial J has two rivals in this cluster — John and Josiah — and R2 refuses both. Josiah's middle initial P contradicts B outright; John's is unrecorded, so nothing decides. Refused by a ratified rule rather than referred: the next pass will refuse it identically and needs no ballot.

research_note: MINTED FROM THE NEWSPAPER REGISTER (T-0376), AND THE HOUSEHOLD IS A CONTAINER RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. Every other record in this dataset argues for a household — a family the sources count, or a trade the town demonstrably needed. This one argues for a PERSON: the Democrat and the American name J. B. Cook as a baker at Chicago 1 time(s), and this reconstruction did not hold them. `data/residents/` has no way to carry a person except inside a household, so one was written around them and told to claim nothing: one member, no dwelling, no division, no origin, no arrival beyond the bound the paper sets. Reading a family, a house or a quarter of town into this record would be reading something the papers do not say. tools/mint_documented_residents.py derives the whole minted set and prints every candidate it refused, with the reason.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.
